actions.justification: Mandatory action: Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned cardiac catheterization. Hydration status assessment is critical to guide pre-procedure IV fluid prophylaxis to prevent contrast-induced nephropathy.

Mandatory action: Baseline eGFR is essential to quantify renal function pre-contrast exposure. CKD stage 4 (eGFR 15-29) places this patient at very high risk for CIN; this result will guide risk stratification and prophylactic measures.

Mandatory action: Systematic review of risk factors (CKD stage 4, diabetes, potential nephrotoxic medications, contrast volume) is required before cardiac catheterization to stratify CIN risk and determine appropriate preventive strategies.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prior to cardiac catheterization. Confirming current hemodynamic stability is essential before proceeding with contrast exposure.
Review current medications to identify nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides) that should be held prior to contrast administration in this high-risk CKD/diabetes patient.
Calculate the maximum safe contrast volume limit based on eGFR to minimize contrast-induced nephropathy risk in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient undergoing cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Evaluating whether alternative imaging (e.g., CO2 angiography, MRI) can be used instead of iodinated contrast is a critical pre-procedural step.
CKD stage 4 with planned cardiac catheterization warrants nephrology input to optimize renal protection strategy, assess risk, and guide peri-procedural management.
Prior to contrast exposure, all nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors/ARBs) should be identified and held to minimize additive renal injury risk in this high-risk patient.
Patient has CKD stage 4 with planned cardiac catheterization — documenting baseline eGFR is essential for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) risk stratification prior to procedure.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced AKI; discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin) before catheterization reduces renal injury risk per CIN prevention guidelines.
Baseline urine output assessment in a CKD stage 4 patient prior to contrast exposure helps establish renal functional reserve and guides pre-procedural hydration strategy.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes. Metformin should be held prior to contrast administration for cardiac catheterization due to risk of lactic acidosis in the setting of contrast-induced nephropathy.

IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid (e.g., normal saline or sodium bicarbonate) is the primary prevention strategy for contrast-induced nephropathy in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization.
Patient with CKD stage 4 may require dose adjustments for renally-cleared medications used during and after cardiac catheterization (e.g., anticoagulants, contrast premedication).

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned contrast exposure — holding nephrotoxic medications reduces risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN). This is distinct from the already-completed 'discontinue_nephrotoxic_agents' step and reinforces ongoing medication review pre-procedure.
Patient has diabetes and CKD stage 4 (likely GFR <45, G3b or worse). Metformin should be held peri-contrast to prevent lactic acidosis risk in setting of potential AKI from contrast exposure.

Pre-planned IV hydration post-contrast is a cornerstone of CIN prevention per nephrology/cardiology guidelines for high-risk patients (CKD + diabetes). Establishing the plan before the procedure ensures timely administration after contrast.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedural IV hydration (isotonic saline) is a key evidence-based intervention to reduce CI-AKI risk before cardiac catheterization, and has not yet been completed.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD/diabetes patient undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of acute kidney injury and guide fluid management.
Post-contrast serum creatinine monitoring at 48-72 hours is guideline-recommended to detect contrast-induced AKI in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes).

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Checking serum creatinine at 48 hours post-contrast is standard protocol to detect AKI early.

Serial creatinine monitoring at 72 hours is recommended in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes) to confirm or rule out contrast-induced nephropathy, as peak creatinine rise may occur up to 72 hours post-contrast.
Patient has CKD stage 4 with diabetes undergoing contrast exposure. Nephrology consultation is warranted for co-management, guidance on renal protection strategies, and planning if AKI develops.
